strengths: Well-motivated dual-space paradigm clearly addressing complementary limitations of feature-space and geometry-space correspondences
Comprehensive experimental validation across three major benchmarks (3DMatch, 3DLoMatch, KITTI) with both hand-crafted and learned features
State-of-the-art precision metrics: best rotation/translation errors on multiple datasets (e.g., RE=1.75°, TE=6.19cm on 3DMatch FPFH)
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3) demonstrating contribution of each component with clear performance degradation when components removed
Extensive robustness analysis including sensitivity to 5 key parameters, varying inlier ratios, and normal estimation variations, showing stable performance across ranges
Thoughtful engineering details including symmetry disambiguation in 1-point RANSAC and probability-weighted refinement
Strong practical efficiency with 32× speedup over MAC and competitive runtimes vs. fastest baselines
High reproducibility: detailed implementation descriptions, algorithm pseudocode, parameter documentation, and supplementary material
Effective speed-accuracy tradeoff balancing precision and computational cost across diverse scenarios
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty—core components (1-point RANSAC, probability-weighted 3-point RANSAC, dual-space weighted optimization) are refinements of prior work (TCF [38], BANSAC [30]) rather than novel methodologies

Actual speedup vs. fastest baseline (TCF) is modest (1.75-1.83× on 3DMatch/3DLoMatch) despite emphasis on efficiency; 32× speedup over MAC is misleading since MAC is inherently slow due to NP-hard clique finding
Registration recall noticeably lower than MAC++ on 3DLoMatch (41.66% vs. 44.58%), suggesting limitations in challenging low-overlap scenarios despite strong precision metrics

Dataset-specific parameter tuning required for optimal performance (α: 0.2→0.95 across datasets, λ: 0.05→1.0), indicating the method is specialized rather than general-purpose despite robustness analysis
Insufficient failure mode analysis—acknowledges struggles with extremely low inlier ratios but lacks empirical characterization of edge cases and failure scenarios
Geometric proxy construction (radius β=50× resolution) chosen empirically without principled theoretical justification; limited comparison with alternative proxy construction methods
No statistical rigor—results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; appears to be single runs rather than multiple trials with variance reporting
Weak comparison with learning-based methods (PointDSC, VBReg) due to GPU time exclusion; may underestimate competitive position of learning approaches on modern hardware
Termination criterion (Eq. 6) depends on estimated inlier ratio which may be unreliable early in iterations; no convergence analysis provided
